The latest evidence on the efficacy of oral phenylephrine as a decongestant is largely negative. Multiple studies and reviews have consistently shown that oral phenylephrine is not significantly more effective than placebo in relieving nasal congestion:

A systematic review and meta-analysis published in 2007 concluded that phenylephrine 10 mg did not significantly affect nasal airway resistance (NAR) compared to placebo, and even at higher doses (25 mg), the evidence was inconsistent and insufficient to support its efficacy.[^(\[1\])]()

Another meta-analysis from the same year found that while phenylephrine 10 mg showed some statistically significant differences compared to placebo, the clinical relevance of these differences was questionable.[^(\[2\])]()

More recent studies have reinforced these findings. A 2015 study evaluating phenylephrine hydrochloride (PE HCl) at doses up to 40 mg found no significant improvement in nasal congestion compared to placebo in patients with seasonal allergic rhinitis.[^(\[3\])]()

Similarly, a 2016 study using modified-release phenylephrine hydrochloride 30 mg tablets also found no significant difference from placebo in relieving nasal congestion.[^(\[4\])]()

The American College of Allergy, Asthma & Immunology, in their 2020 practice parameter update on rhinitis, explicitly states that oral phenylephrine has been demonstrated to be ineffective at reducing nasal congestion at doses up to 40 mg.[^(\[5\])]()

1.[Efficacy and Safety of Oral Phenylephrine: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17264159) Hatton RC, Winterstein AG, McKelvey RP, Shuster J, Hendeles L. The Annals of Pharmacotherapy. 2007;41(3):381-90. doi:10.1345/aph.1H679.
